query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the local variations in chemical order—through the creation of heterogeneous lattice strain fields—synergistically increase hardness and yield strength by pinning dislocations via fluctuating local shear‐fault energies and lattice friction. In effect, regions with enhanced short-range order produce more rugged dislocation slip paths and elevated energy barriers, thereby improving strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeNi or NiCoCr) in its homogenized, as-cast state with typical grain sizes.
generation.intervention: Process identical alloy compositions under two different thermal-mechanical treatments: one route promotes enhanced local chemical ordering (e.g., moderate annealing that allows short-range order to form without precipitating a new phase), and the other route promotes a nearly random (disordered) solid solution (e.g., via rapid quenching or severe plastic deformation).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature and under moderate strain rates where dislocation-mediated plasticity prevails. Grain size and overall phase remain constant between samples so that differences arise predominantly from internal chemical ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical order (LCO) and associated heterogeneous lattice strain fields that lead to spatial fluctuations in the local shear‐fault energy.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced local ordering creates regions of heightened lattice distortion and fluctuating shear-fault energies that act as strong pinning sites for dislocations. This increases the effective energy barrier for dislocation glide and promotes dislocation entanglement, meaning that dislocations are forced to follow more tortuous, ‘roughened’ pathways. In contrast, a nearly random solid solution displays a more uniform lattice strain field, with lower effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy processed to enhance local chemical order will exhibit a higher yield strength and indentation hardness compared to the chemically disordered baseline. Microscopy (e.g., TEM or atom probe) should reveal more pronounced dislocation pinning and irregular slip paths in the LCO-enhanced sample.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy processed to minimize local chemical order (random solid solution) with a homogeneous lattice strain field.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where dislocation motion dominates plastic deformation (e.g., low-to-moderate temperatures and strain rates). At very high temperatures or extremely high strain rates—where diffusion or dynamic recovery plays a major role—the contribution from LCO-induced heterogeneous lattice strains may be reduced or masked by other mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines evidence on heterogeneous lattice strain strengthening (e.g., PMC9231497::web::000::abstract, PMC6687833::web::000::abstract) with findings on dislocation turbulence and local ordering effects (e.g., PMC10990144::web::000::abstract, PMC10041143::web::000::abstract). While each effect has been observed individually, their direct synergistic contribution to hardness and yield strength remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples (of identical composition and grain size) by applying two processing routes: one to promote local chemical order (e.g., controlled annealing at an intermediate temperature for sufficient time) and another to maintain a random solid solution (e.g., rapid quenching or severe plastic deformation). Perform tensile and nanoindentation tests to measure yield strength and hardness, and use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography to characterize dislocation patterns and quantify the degree of local chemical order.
measurements: Dislocation density and slip path roughness observed with TEM
Degree of local chemical ordering measured by atom probe tomography or diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with promoted local chemical order do not exhibit significantly higher yield strength/hardness and do not show evidence of more rugged dislocation paths (i.e., comparable dislocation density and slip behavior to the randomized samples), then the hypothesis that LCO-induced heterogeneous lattice strains govern the enhanced hardness and strength is falsified.

Our work shows the underlying physical characteristics of chemical short-range order in multi-principal element alloys, which causes higher strain peaks and wider strain wavelengths compared to traditional alloys. Remarkably, the heterogeneous lattice strain field induces a unique dislocation turbulent behavior and forms a special dislocation structure that is both a source and a trap at the vortex point, significantly enhancing both strength and ductility. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. SignificanceMulti–principal element alloys exhibit outstanding mechanical properties owing to severe atomic lattice distortion. However, the heterogeneous strain caused by lattice distortion at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale has been ignored for a long time because the heterogeneous strain field is difficult to quantify and characterize. Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms, leading to the strength-ductility synergy in severely distorted compositionally complex crystals. Multi–principal element alloys (MPEAs) exhibit outstanding mechanical properties because the core effect of severe atomic lattice distortion is distinctly different from that of traditional alloys. However, at the mesoscopic scale the underlying physics for the abundant dislocation activities responsible for strength-ductility synergy has not been uncovered.
